issues.description: The manuscript states the SESOI is δ=.27 in one place but then states it was set equal to a β value of .11 and refers to the equivalence region as δ=|.11|. These are contradictory specifications of the same parameter, and a reader cannot determine which value will actually be used in the equivalence test. This is a critical analytic specification in a Registered Report, where the analytic plan must be precisely fixed in advance.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.description: The Present Study section defines moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval with the FREQUENCY of engaging in the behavior, consistent with the rest of the manuscript. However, the methods later state moral incongruence will be measured as the interaction of moral disapproval with SEVERITY OF CONSEQUENCES from the action. These are fundamentally different constructs (frequency of use vs. severity of consequences), and the latter would conflate the predictor with the outcome (problematic use). This contradiction undermines the central operationalization of the study.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.description: For substances, the outcome (problematic use) is computed by averaging NIDA-ASSIST items, some of which are themselves frequency-of-use-related (e.g., 'strong desire or urge to use,' 'failed to control, cut down or stop'). The focal predictor is behavioral frequency. When frequency-laden items are used as the outcome and frequency is the predictor, the interaction term may be confounded with shared method/content variance, inflating or distorting effects and undermining construct distinctiveness between predictor and outcome.
issues.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST.

issues.description: The substance 'problematic use' composite averages three items on a 0-5 scale with two items on a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging items with different numeric ranges and anchors without standardization gives disproportionate weight to the 0/3/6 items and produces a composite of ambiguous metric. No mention is made of rescaling or standardizing these items before averaging.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.description: The frequency predictor uses a past-12-month window, the NIDA-ASSIST problematic-use items use past-3-month windows, the BPS uses a past-6-month window, and the PGSI uses a past-12-month window. Combining predictors and outcomes assessing different time frames within the same interaction model creates temporal misalignment that can attenuate or distort the frequency-by-disapproval interaction and complicates interpretation.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use (“In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?”

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent frequency scale anchoring (0 vs 1 start)
issues.description: The text describes the frequency scale inconsistently: substances are described as 0 (never) to 5, pornography as 1 (never) to 6, and gambling as 1 (never) to 6, while supplemental tables show 0 (never) to 5 for all. These inconsistencies in scale anchoring affect centering and the construction/interpretation of interaction terms and must be fixed precisely in a registered analytic plan.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.description: The stated goal is explicitly to 'demonstrate' a predetermined conclusion rather than to test it neutrally. Framing a Registered Report around demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior signals confirmation-oriented reasoning, which is concerning given that the entire inferential structure relies on accepting null/equivalence results for other behaviors.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.description: The core inference—that moral incongruence is 'unique' to pornography—rests on finding significant interactions for pornography AND equivalence-to-null interactions for all other behaviors. Establishing 'uniqueness' requires a direct test of the difference between the pornography interaction and each other interaction (e.g., a moderated comparison or interaction-of-interactions), not separate significant vs. equivalence results in different models with different sample sizes and outcome measures. Comparing a significant result in one model to a non-significant/equivalent result in another is a known inferential error.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.description: The plan permits switching the equivalence region to the lower bound of a 95% CI from a prior study if the primary SESOI test fails or is underpowered. Allowing the equivalence bound to be redefined contingent on results (or on power) introduces researcher degrees of freedom that can be used to obtain equivalence conclusions, weakening the confirmatory nature of the Registered Report.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors assume no missing data and no need to remove careless responders based on vendor assurances. This is implausible for a 4,000-person survey with many sensitive items (substance use, pornography, gambling). No missing-data handling plan (e.g., MI, FIML), no attention-check plan, and no contingency for nonresponse are provided, threatening replicability and the validity of complete-case analyses.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction on who completes problematic-use measures
issues.description: One section states only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further problematic-use measures, while a later section states problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to ALL participants regardless of engagement. These mutually exclusive procedures change the effective sample, the meaning of the frequency-by-disapproval interaction (e.g., inclusion of zeros), and the analyses, and must be resolved.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.description: The total sample includes a 1,500-person sports-wagering oversample, making gambling behavior non-representative (the power table even lists gambling as 100% for the oversample and an effective N of 3,325). Combining a representative sample with a targeted oversample without describing weighting for the gambling analyses threatens representativeness and the comparability of the gambling interaction to other behaviors.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73%  (national sample) 100%  (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval may not capture moral incongruence
issues.description: Moral disapproval is measured with a single item per behavior ('I believe that X is morally wrong'). Single-item measures have unknown/unestimable reliability, and a single global wrongness judgment may not capture personalized moral incongruence (disapproval of one's OWN behavior). This is the central moderator of the study, so measurement weakness here is consequential.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.description: The authors add pornography and gambling to the NIDA-ASSIST and claim parallelism, while acknowledging this is not validated. The assertion that including non-validated items 'will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses' is unsupported; using an unvalidated outcome for substances (and as a parallel outcome for pornography) directly affects the central comparison the study rests upon.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring/anchors inconsistent with validated instrument and within manuscript
issues.description: The supplemental PGSI table uses response anchors 0/2/4/5 (Never/Sometimes/Most of the time/Almost Always), which is non-standard (the validated PGSI uses 0-1-2-3). The main text states the PGSI uses a 0-3 scale and that responses will be averaged, whereas the PGSI is conventionally summed for severity categories. These inconsistencies in scoring affect score meaning, comparability to norms, and the dependent variable's metric.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., “Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?” and “Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?”) on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.description: The main text describes the Brief Pornography Screen as a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often) with responses summed, but the supplemental BPS table uses anchors 0 (Never), 2 (Occasionally), 4 (Very Often). The scale anchoring (0-1-2 vs 0-2-4) changes the summed score range and comparability to the validated BPS cut scores.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between covariate description and gender coding
issues.description: Gender is described as a covariate and later coded as binary (1 = male, 0 = not-male), but the supplemental substance items branch on 'GENDER = WOMAN' and 'GENDER = MAN,' implying a different/categorical coding and excluding non-binary respondents from the binge-drinking branching. The handling of gender (binary vs. multi-category; treatment of 'not-male') is underspecified and internally inconsistent, affecting both covariate modeling and item routing.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: Binge-drinking item label contradicts gender-specific threshold
issues.description: The supplemental binge-drinking items present different thresholds by gender (more than 4 drinks for women, more than 5 for men), but both response rows are labeled 'More than four drinks (1).' The item label contradicts the stated stem for men and could produce measurement error in alcohol assessment.
issues.quote: In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?

issues.description: By the authors' own power table, prescription drug misuse (projected n=140) and illicit drug use (n=240-480) are underpowered to detect the primary SESOI (achieved power .301 and .472-.764). Drawing equivalence (null) conclusions in underpowered cells risks false equivalence claims; the proposed remedy is to switch to a much larger equivalence bound, which only allows weaker inferences. This undermines the ability to support the central uniqueness claim for these substances.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301

issues.description: Although a limitation about cross-sectional data is briefly noted, much of the manuscript uses directional language (moral incongruence 'amplifies,' 'drives,' 'predicts,' 'contributes to' feelings of addiction) and frames implications as if temporal/causal precedence were established. With a single-wave correlational design, the interaction cannot establish that disapproval amplifies use-addiction links rather than reflecting reverse or third-variable processes.
issues.quote: In short, moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction.

issues.description: Low-prevalence behaviors (illicit drugs, prescription misuse) and rare problematic-use endorsements will produce highly skewed, zero-inflated outcomes, yet the plan relies on OLS regression with only vague mention of 'supplemental analyses' if assumptions are 'substantially violated.' No pre-specified criteria, transformation, or alternative model (e.g., count/zero-inflated models) are defined, leaving substantial analytic flexibility and threatening valid inference.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.description: The decision rule for presenting OLS vs. supplemental analyses depends on whether results 'remain robust' (same sign and significance), but the specific alternative methods, the threshold for 'substantial' assumption violations, and the order of operations are not pre-specified. This leaves room for selective reporting in a confirmatory report.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices/supplemental materials.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of ICD-11 CSBD exclusion rationale
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames its hypotheses as supporting the ICD-11 'decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration,' but the ICD-11 caveat is an exclusion clarifying that moral distress alone is insufficient for diagnosis. The reasoning that confirming uniqueness of moral incongruence to sexual behavior would 'corroborate' the caveat is a conceptual leap: the caveat's justification is clinical (avoiding pathologizing moral distress), not contingent on moral incongruence being statistically unique to sex relative to substances.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis effective N assumptions not justified
issues.description: Effective Ns in Table 2 are derived by applying single-behavior prevalence estimates to the total sample, but this does not account for the conditional sampling (only users complete outcomes), the sports-bettor oversample for non-gambling behaviors, covariate missingness, or the contradiction about who completes measures. The basis for the listed effective Ns is therefore not transparent or fully justified.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | 60% | 2,400 | .003 | .999

issues.subcategory: Religiousness composite direction and standardization details
issues.description: Religiousness is built from three Pew items with reverse-coded raw values, standardized, averaged, then multiplied by -1. Combining items with different numbers of response options via standardization is reasonable, but no reliability evidence, factor structure, or justification for equal weighting is provided for this composite that serves as a key covariate (and theoretically a proxy for moral disapproval). Given the model leans heavily on religiousness, more validation detail is needed.
issues.quote: Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center (Pew Research Center, 2015).

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis numbering referenced but not defined
issues.description: The analytic plan refers to 'hypotheses 2b and 3b' as the equivalence hypotheses, but the hypotheses in the Present Study section are presented as prose paragraphs without the 2b/3b labeling. Readers cannot reliably map the equivalence-test inferences onto specific numbered hypotheses, reducing transparency about which confirmatory tests support which predictions.
issues.quote: thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b, listed above.

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency averaged across heterogeneous activities undefined
issues.description: The main text says gambling frequency will be an 'average across gambling behaviors,' implying multiple gambling-activity frequency items, but the supplemental materials contain only a single global gambling-frequency item. It is unclear whether one item or multiple items will be collected, which affects the predictor's construction and the meaning of 'average.'
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: Multiplicity across eight outcomes not addressed for interactions
issues.description: Eight interaction models are tested as the central confirmatory analyses, and bivariate correlations are Holm-adjusted, but no correction or family-wise error strategy is specified for the eight focal interaction tests. Given the uniqueness claim depends on a particular pattern across many tests, the absence of a multiplicity plan for the primary tests is a reporting gap.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Self-reported 'feelings of addiction' generalized to clinical diagnosis
issues.description: The study measures self-reported/self-perceived feelings of addiction in a community sample, yet the discussion extends implications to clinical diagnosis (false-positive CSBD diagnoses) and to validating the ICD-11 caveat. The authors partly acknowledge this, but the framing throughout overextends population-level self-report findings to treatment-seeking and diagnostic contexts where the constructs and base rates differ.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.
